summary: Describes a framework for supporting IETF Integrated Services on shared and switched IEEE 802 LAN infrastructure. It sets out the concepts that companion documents use for admission control and service mapping. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the big-picture plan for giving some traffic a reserved lane on local networks. It explains the ideas, and other documents fill in the details.

questions: qos on shared and switched lans
how to support quality of service on local networks
integrated services over ethernet and token ring
subtitle: How to bring quality-of-service guarantees to enterprise local networks.

tldr.problem: Local area networks lack the resource management mechanisms to support real-time applications like video conferencing that need guaranteed latency and throughput. Best-effort service treats all traffic equally.
tldr.mechanism: The Bandwidth Manager architecture separates resource management into a Requester Module at end stations and a Bandwidth Allocator that performs admission control. Switches use traffic classes (priority queues) and signaling protocols to enforce reservations across the LAN.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can offer service guarantees on campus networks and the last hop to the Internet, bridging between IETF Integrated Services IP standards and the IEEE 802 link layer technologies already deployed in LANs.

today: This framework remains active in standards work. It has influenced how modern campus networks and data centers manage QoS. However, simpler approaches (like Differentiated Services, which marks packets but does not require per-flow state) have seen wider deployment than the per-flow reservation model this document describes.

sections.title: The Problem: QoS on Local Networks
sections.content:
The Internet and most LANs offer best-effort service: they deliver packets as quickly as possible but make no promises about delay, jitter (variation in delay), or whether packets arrive at all. Real-time applications such as video conferencing, Internet telephony and live streaming cannot tolerate such uncertainty.

The IETF's Integrated Services framework defines how routers and hosts can reserve bandwidth and enforce service guarantees. However, LANs built on IEEE 802 technologies (Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI) were not designed with resource management in mind. Simply running RSVP over a shared Ethernet segment does not guarantee anything because the link layer has no queuing or admission control.

This memo describes how to bring Integrated Services guarantees down to the LAN layer, where the last hop to the user and the entire enterprise campus network can enforce them.
sections.plainLanguage: Your office network is like a single shared hallway where everyone walks at once. This document explains how to give important messages a separate, less crowded path so they get through faster and more reliably.

sections.title: LAN Technologies and Priority
sections.content:
Different IEEE 802 LAN technologies offer different QoS capabilities. Ethernet (802.3) has no built-in priority mechanism unless you add an external tag (802.1Q). Token Ring (802.5) carries a 3-bit User Priority field that stations and bridges can use to queue frames at different priority levels. FDDI and Demand Priority (802.12) also support priority mechanisms.

All these technologies support a concept called traffic classes—separate queues at each switch port, each served at a different priority. Token Ring explicitly reserves the token for high-priority traffic. Demand Priority promises that high-priority frames access the medium before normal-priority ones.

The framework maps the eight priority levels (0 to 7, where 7 is highest) onto however many queues the switch actually implements. A simple switch might have just two queues (high and low). A sophisticated one might have eight.
sections.plainLanguage: Some office networks (like Ethernet) do not have built-in lanes, while others (like Token Ring) already number traffic from 0 (slow) to 7 (fast). Switches use these numbers to decide which queue to put a message in.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Manager Model
sections.content:
The Bandwidth Manager is divided into three parts. The Requester Module runs on every end station (host or router) that wants to make reservations. It translates requests from the application or from RSVP into a form the LAN can understand, and reports back success or failure.

The Bandwidth Allocator makes the admission control decision: Is there enough bandwidth on the path from sender to receiver? It can be implemented centrally (one decision engine for the entire subnet) or distributed (each switch makes its own local decisions). A centralized approach is simpler to deploy but does not scale well. A distributed approach scales better but requires upgrades to every switch.

The Allocator must also decide which traffic class or priority level to assign to the reserved flow. It returns this choice to the Requester Module, which tags outgoing packets with the appropriate priority in the LAN header.

The third component is the communication protocol between modules. The memo describes this in terms of the Subnet Bandwidth Manager (SBM) protocol, a specialization of RSVP for LANs, but the concepts work with any signaling mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the Bandwidth Manager as a three-part system: a requester at your desk that asks for reservations, an allocator that decides if there is room, and messages flowing back and forth to confirm the deal.

sections.title: How Switches Support Reservations
sections.content:
A switch supporting Integrated Services over LANs must perform several functions. When a reservation request arrives at an ingress (input) port, the switch's admission control module checks whether the link has free bandwidth. If yes, the request passes to the propagation module, which forwards it to the switch's egress (output) ports where the flow is heading.

Each output port also runs admission control. Only if all hops accept the request is the reservation confirmed. The switch's classifier module identifies incoming packets by their priority or other headers and places them in the appropriate queue. The queue and scheduler serve the queues in priority order (or another algorithm like weighted fair queuing), ensuring high-priority traffic gets out on time.

Optional modules can police traffic (drop packets that exceed the agreed bandwidth) or remap priority values as the packet moves from one type of link to another (for example, from a Token Ring to an Ethernet segment).
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch port acts like a post office: it checks if a package fits the reservation, marks it with its agreed priority, and makes sure high-priority packages get shipped first.

sections.title: Design Challenges and Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The memo lists key requirements: resource reservation, admission control, flow separation and scheduling, traffic policing, soft state (refreshing reservations periodically), and support for both centralized and distributed implementations. It must scale to large subnets and tolerate switch failures.

A major design decision is whether to police traffic at switches or trust end stations to police themselves. The framework chooses to trust end stations (for simplicity) and asks switches to merely mark and queue packets. If an end station cheats and sends faster than agreed, the switch does not explicitly stop it but may remap its priority down.

Another challenge is receiver heterogeneity: in a multicast group, different receivers might want different service levels. Some want low latency, others just best-effort. The framework addresses this by allowing multiple separate reservations to the same group or by supporting different filter styles.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes a balancing act: making the system simple to deploy, able to grow, and fair to all users, while letting end stations decide how hard to push on their reserved bandwidth.
